content:
We're excited to present Choir, an open protocol for coordinating multi-agent autoformalization.

With Choir, you plan a formalization project with your own orchestrator agent, and anyone can take on its tasks with their own AI agent and LLM subscription. Choir handles all the coordination in between.

Choir gives you full autonomy: it runs on your own GitHub repository, and you control how the project operates.

Choir is open source under Apache-2.0 and designed to be modular. We hope people can build their own framework on it or plug it into an existing workflow.

  • Code and how to use: https://github.com/Weber-GeoML/Choir
  • Paper: https://github.com/Weber-GeoML/Choir/blob/main/paper/choir.pdf

  • Demo: a formalization of Yufei Zhao's Probabilistic Methods in Combinatorics
    https://github.com/yidiq7/ProbMethodCombinatorics

  • Visualization of the demo: https://yidiq7.github.io/ProbMethodCombinatorics/choir-proof-tree.html

Choir is supported by the DARPA expMath program.

Hi Yidi, nice paper!

I noticed in your introduction and related work section you reference Meta's AutoformBot (which I am currently maintaining) and @Kunal Marwaha's Prove2Me system. I think the general architecture in Figure 1 and CLI tool in table 2 is very similar to what I have been developing for FAIR. On the other hand, the decomposition protocol described on pg. 4 is reminiscent of Prove2me's system. The timeline visualization is something I have not yet considered, but I've seen @Vasily Ilin play around with similar animations like with his Green-Tao Demo.

I think that we are all trying to converge on a similar framework, so if you have any ideas for how we can collaborate on autoformalization tooling I'd love to know.

Thanks Jack! Choir actually started from FAIR's work: when RepoProver came out we were very excited, but the cost was out of reach for academic groups so we tried to extend the architecture to a distributed system. But back then the code was under CC BY-NC so we ended up writing our own with open-source license. I hadn't looked closely at the new version of AutoformBot until now, and you are right that many of our design choices are close.

And thanks for mentioning @Vasily Ilin's work. I hadn't seen it before and it looks very elegant. In our case, during testing, we found that the orchestrator was doing most of the work, which is the opposite of what we intended. So we added decomposition with visualization to monitor which agent did what. The final version ended up close to Prove2Me's system. I was wondering if you observed similar things with AutoformBot's orchestrator-worker design?

I agree we are converging on a similar framework and we should definitely collaborate! One thing I asked Claude was that if it could plug in Choir's task distribution component into AutoformBot to make it a distributed system. It seems to be quite straightforward with some minor changes. Happy to discuss more, and maybe we could meet in person at some point!

Yidi Qi said:

One thing I asked Claude was that if it could plug in Choir's task distribution component into AutoformBot to make it a distributed system. It seems to be quite straightforward with some minor changes.

Yes that would be amazing! We are totally open to external PRs to AutoformBot if you manage to set this up please open one. I'd love for all of our systems to interoperate with each other. I'll reach out privately where we can discuss further.

We added a short integration note to Choir, and AutoformBot and Choir should now work together. Nothing needs to be changed on the AutoformBot side. One can still use the usual AutoformBot prompt and simply add a line like "Use Choir to distribute the tasks and act as the orchestrator (or join <repo> as a worker)". I have only done small tests so far, so let me know if you would like to do some larger-scale testing together! @Jack McCarthy
